content.content:
1	# ChronicleFlow
2	
3	ChronicleFlow is a small backend for durable workflow orchestration. It stores
4	workflow definitions, execution state, and an append-only event history in
5	SQLite so an execution can be inspected and replayed deterministically.
6	
7	The initial release intentionally supports a compact public contract:
8	
9	- workflows are directed acyclic graphs of `task`, `condition`, bounded
10	  `loop`, and dynamic `map` nodes;
11	- a workflow may declare named versions: every declared version is kept and
12	  each execution is bound to the version that was current (or explicitly
13	  named) when it started, so upgrading a workflow never changes a running
14	  execution, and a running execution can be explicitly migrated to another
15	  version of the same workflow, after which it advances under that version;
16	- executions advance one ready task at a time, evaluating conditions and
17	  skipping unmatched branches automatically;
18	- task nodes may declare a bounded number of retries: a submitted failure
19	  re-queues the node until the retries are exhausted, which terminates the
20	  execution;
21	- a task node may declare an approval point with the people allowed to decide
22	  it; advancing parks the task in a waiting state until an approver approves
23	  (completing it with the submitted output) or rejects (terminating the
24	  execution with reason `rejected`);
25	- executions may declare a timeout in seconds, after which they terminate and
26	  no longer accept output, and they may be cancelled explicitly;
27	- loop nodes repeat their body a bounded number of times, re-evaluating a
28	  continue condition at the loop boundaries;
29	- a map node inside a loop body expands independently in every iteration
30	  from that iteration's source output, its instances and events belonging
31	  to the iteration they expanded in;
32	- every state transition is appended to the execution event stream;
33	- replay rebuilds execution state from the recorded events;
34	- a checkpoint is written at every node boundary, capturing the state
35	  summary and event position, so an execution can be recovered from the
36	  latest checkpoint after a restart;
37	- workers may claim a running execution to receive a work item with a
38	  time-bounded lease, renew the lease with heartbeats, and release it;
39	  while a lease is active only its holder may submit results, and an
40	  expired or released lease returns the work item to the claimable set;
41	- duplicate commands with the same idempotency key return the original result;
42	- workflows and executions may declare webhook subscriptions, and matching
43	  business events are delivered to the declared targets with bounded retries,
44	  each delivery recorded in a per-execution history;
45	- subscriptions may also declare queue targets instead of webhook addresses:
46	  matching business events are appended, in occurrence order, to persistent
47	  per-execution queues that callers pull from and acknowledge explicitly,
48	  with a visibility timeout returning unacknowledged messages to the pending
49	  set (delivery is at least once);
50	- a workflow may declare a schedule — a fixed interval in seconds or a
51	  five-field cron plan — and the service automatically creates one execution
52	  per due period with the declared input; schedules can be paused and
53	  resumed, periods missed while paused are either caught up once or
54	  skipped, according to the declared missed policy, and a read-only preview
55	  query projects the upcoming trigger times and their inputs.
56	
57	## Requirements
58	
59	- Python 3.11 or newer
60	- no third-party runtime dependencies
61	
62	## Run the service
63	
64	```bash
65	PYTHONPATH=src python -m chronicleflow.server --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 --database chronicleflow.db
66	```
67	
68	The process prints `ChronicleFlow listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080` after it
69	has bound the port.
70	
71	## HTTP API
72	
73	All request and response bodies are JSON. Unknown fields are rejected.
74	
75	Responses are compact JSON with no insignificant whitespace, and every
76	response body ends with exactly one trailing newline (`\n`). Numbers
77	round-trip with their full precision: finite floats keep their original
78	IEEE-754 value through the shortest textual representation that decodes to
79	it (so `0.30000000000000004` stays `0.30000000000000004`), negative zero is
80	preserved as `-0.0`, and integers stay integers. Non-finite numbers may
81	never appear in a request and are never produced in a response; timestamps
82	are ISO-8601 UTC strings ending in `Z`.
83	
84	### Tenants and quotas
85	
86	A request may declare a tenant by sending the `X-Tenant-Id` header with a
87	non-empty identifier. Every workflow, execution, schedule, schedule status,
88	delivery history, and queue record is scoped to the tenant of the request that
89	created it: queries and operations only ever see data belonging to that
90	tenant, and different tenants may use the same workflow or execution
91	identifiers without colliding. Referencing another tenant's resource — for
92	example advancing, migrating, deciding, claiming, cancelling, recovering, replaying, or
93	reading the events, checkpoints, deliveries, queues, or schedule of an execution or
94	workflow owned by another tenant, or pulling from or acknowledging one of its
95	queues — is answered exactly like a reference to a
96	missing resource: `404 not_found`, with no indication that the resource
97	exists elsewhere. An execution created in one tenant can only reference a
98	workflow of the same tenant, and a migration can only name a version of that
99	workflow in the same tenant; referencing an unseen workflow identifier or
100	version is the usual `404 not_found`.
101	
102	The header applies to every workflow, execution, and schedule entry point,
103	including creation, advancement, migration, approval decisions, lease
104	operations, cancellation, recovery, replay, instance deletion and
105	modification and re-expansion, queue pulls, acknowledgements, and all
106	history and status queries, as well as the usage, bill, and metrics queries. An empty
107	`X-Tenant-Id` value is a `400 validation_error`. Requests that omit the
108	header entirely keep using the single legacy namespace, whose advancement,
109	approvals, leases, retries, timeouts, cancellation, checkpoints, recovery,
110	scheduling, and replay behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged: the tenant is
111	stored only as database scope, never added to a state field or event payload,
112	and state shapes and event streams gain no new fields. Idempotency keys are
113	scoped per tenant as well, so tenants can never see or collide with each
114	other's keys; reusing a key for another operation within the same tenant is
115	the usual `409 conflict`.
116	
117	A tenant may declare quotas bounding how many workflows and executions it may
118	hold:
119	
120	```http
121	PUT /quotas
122	Idempotency-Key: quota-request-1
123	X-Tenant-Id: acme
124	
125	{"workflows": 10, "executions": 100}
126	```
127	
128	`POST` to the same path is accepted as well. The body must contain exactly
129	`workflows` and `executions`, each a positive integer; a non-positive,
130	non-integer, boolean, or non-finite value, a missing or extra field, or a
131	non-object body is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Both quota
132	routes require a tenant: calling them without `X-Tenant-Id` (or with an empty
133	one) is a `400 validation_error`. The response is
134	`{"quota":{"workflows":10,"executions":100}}`; declaring again replaces the
135	limits (re-anchoring nothing else). Lowering a limit below the current
136	holding deletes no existing data — existing workflows and executions stay
137	fully usable — it only rejects later writes that would exceed the new limit.
138	
139	```http
140	GET /quotas
141	X-Tenant-Id: acme
142	```
143	
144	Returns the declared quota, or the definite empty result `{"quota":null}`
145	when the tenant has declared none.
146	
147	When a write would take the tenant past either limit, the whole request is
148	rejected with `409 conflict` and an error message that names the quota (for
149	example `quota exceeded: tenant already holds 10 workflows (quota limit is
150	10)`), so callers can tell quota rejection apart from an ordinary identifier
151	conflict. The rejection performs no partial write: nothing is inserted and
152	previously stored data is unaffected, exactly as for validation failures.
153	
154	A schedule firing on time creates its execution in the schedule's tenant and
155	that execution counts against the tenant's execution quota. When the tenant
156	is at its execution limit, the due period creates no execution and the
157	schedule is left unchanged — its cursor, `last_triggered_at`, and
158	`last_execution_id` stay as they were — so the period is settled on a later
159	pass once capacity exists, under the usual per-period idempotence. Delivery
160	history follows the tenant of the execution it belongs to.
161	
162	### Usage metering and billing
163	
164	Requests that carry a tenant identifier leave a usage record for each billable
165	action they perform. Only tenant-scoped requests are metered: a request that
166	omits the `X-Tenant-Id` header keeps the legacy namespace and writes no usage
167	record at all, with its state shapes and event content unchanged. The four
168	metered action types are:
169	
170	- `workflow_created` — a workflow definition is stored. Adding a new version
171	  to an existing workflow is one workflow creation, the same as the first
172	  definition;
173	- `execution_started` — an execution is created and starts `running`;
174	- `schedule_triggered` — a due schedule period creates its execution. The
175	  scheduled execution is metered both as `execution_started` and as
176	  `schedule_triggered`;
177	- `delivery_attempted` — one outbound webhook HTTP attempt is made, or one
178	  queue message is delivered to a caller pulling from a queue. A
179	  subscription that retries is metered once per attempt, so a delivery that
180	  fails and then succeeds on its second attempt records two attempts; the
181	  action is metered whether it ultimately succeeds or fails. A queue pull
182	  meters one attempt per message it delivers, so a redelivery after the
183	  visibility timeout is metered again, while a pull that delivers nothing
184	  meters nothing.
185	
186	Metering is atomic with the action it describes: a write rejected by
187	validation or by a quota produces no record and performs no partial write.
188	Repeating an idempotent command returns its first result and writes no second
189	record, and settling the same schedule period more than once (a repeated
190	trigger or a later pass) meters that period only once. Replay, recovery, and
191	queries never meter and never alter recorded usage or billing conclusions.
192	
193	```http
194	GET /usage
195	X-Tenant-Id: acme
196	```
197	
198	Returns `{"usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}`: the
199	cumulative count of recorded actions per type, sorted by ascending type
200	identifier. Types with no records are omitted, so a tenant with no usage gets
201	the definite empty result `{"usage":[]}`.
202	
203	```http
204	GET /bill
205	X-Tenant-Id: acme
206	```
207	
208	Returns the per-type bill:
209	
210	```json
211	{"bill":{"items":[
212	  {"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100},
213	  {"type":"workflow_created","count":2,"unit_price":1000,"subtotal":2000}
214	],"total":2100}}
215	```
216	
217	Each item gives the metered `count`, a positive-integer `unit_price` in cents
218	that is also returned in the response, and a `subtotal` equal to
219	`count * unit_price`; `total` is the integer-cent sum of every subtotal. With
220	no records, `items` is empty and `total` is `0`.
221	
222	Both endpoints accept the same optional query parameters the events and
223	metrics queries accept: an optional metered-type filter and an ISO-8601 UTC
224	timestamp window, each timestamp ending in `Z`, plus an optional fixed time
225	bucket:
226	
227	```http
228	GET /usage?type=execution_started,workflow_created&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
229	GET /bill?type=execution_started&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
230	X-Tenant-Id: acme
231	```
232	
233	- `type` names one metered action type or a comma-separated set of them; only
234	  records whose type is in the set are counted. A single identifier needs no
235	  comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown metered type is a
236	  `400 validation_error`; when `type` is absent every type is counted, exactly
237	  as before;
238	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on each usage record's
239	  occurrence time: a record whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted.
240	  When either parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting
241	  both returns exactly the cumulative result above;
242	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
243	  parameter is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing;
244	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
245	  simply contains no records. Usage then reports the definite empty result
246	  `{"usage":[]}`, and the bill reports an empty `items` list with a `total` of
247	  `0`.
248	
249	The type filter and the time window apply together as an intersection: a
250	record is counted only when its type is named **and** its occurrence time is
251	in the window. A type the filter names but that has no matching record is
252	omitted rather than reported at zero, so a filter that matches nothing gives
253	the same definite empty results as an empty window: `{"usage":[]}` for usage
254	and an empty `items` list with a `total` of `0` for the bill.
255	
256	Both endpoints also accept an optional `bucket` parameter for a fixed-bucket
257	trend summary, so callers never have to pull records and group them
258	themselves:
259	
260	```http
261	GET /usage?bucket=hour&since=2026-09-26T00:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-27T00:00:00.000Z
262	GET /bill?bucket=day&type=execution_started
263	X-Tenant-Id: acme
264	```
265	
266	- `bucket` is exactly `hour` or `day`: `hour` buckets start on the UTC hour
267	  and `day` buckets at UTC midnight, both aligned solely to UTC. An empty or
268	  any other value is a `400 validation_error`, exactly like a repeated
269	  parameter or an unknown query parameter;
270	- when `bucket` is present, usage returns
271	  `{"usage_buckets":[{"bucket_start":"2026-09-26T08:00:00Z","usage":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1}, ...]}, ...]}`:
272	  the buckets with at least one matching record, in ascending bucket-start
273	  order. Each entry gives its `bucket_start` first — an ISO-8601 UTC string
274	  ending in `Z` at the hour or midnight — followed by `usage`, the per-type
275	  counts inside that bucket in ascending type-identifier order; a type with no
276	  record in the bucket is omitted;
277	- when `bucket` is present, the bill returns
278	  `{"bill":{"buckets":[{"bucket_start":"2026-09-26T00:00:00Z","items":[{"type":"execution_started","count":1,"unit_price":100,"subtotal":100}, ...],"subtotal":100}, ...],"total":100}}`.
279	  Buckets appear in ascending bucket-start order; each bucket's `items` stay
280	  sorted by ascending type identifier, each line giving the filtered count,
281	  the usual positive-integer `unit_price`, and an integer-cent `subtotal` of
282	  the two, and a type with no matching record is omitted rather than reported
283	  at zero. Each bucket also carries its own `subtotal`, and the window
284	  `total` is exactly the sum of the listed per-bucket subtotals, all amounts
285	  integer cents;
286	- a bucket that holds no matching record never appears, so an empty tenant, a
287	  window with `since` later than `until`, or a filter that matches nothing
288	  returns the definite empty bucket lists `{"usage_buckets":[]}` and
289	  `{"bill":{"buckets":[],"total":0}` — never an error, with the empty bill's
290	  total at `0`;
291	- bucketing applies together with the type filter and the time window as an
292	  intersection: a bucket holds only records whose occurrence time is in the
293	  closed window **and** whose type the filter names. The window keeps its
294	  closed endpoints, its open bounds when either side is omitted, and the
295	  existing rule for when a record's instant falls in it; buckets are simply
296	  the same matching records rolled up to their UTC bucket;
297	- the bucketed queries are read-only like the others: they append no usage
298	  records, change no metering basis or prices, and never alter recorded usage
299	  or billing conclusions — under event replay or recovery the same window,
300	  type filter, and bucket always give the same answer;
301	- omitting `bucket` leaves both queries exactly as before: the same compact
302	  JSON responses with `usage` / `items` shapes, full float precision and the
303	  `-0.0` convention, byte for byte. The parameter introduces no second
304	  protocol and changes no entry point's existing behavior.
305	
306	Only records whose occurrence time falls in the window are counted. Within
307	the window the bill keeps the same basis as always: each present type reports
308	its filtered, windowed count, its usual `unit_price`, and a `subtotal` of the
309	two; items stay sorted by ascending type identifier, and a type with no
310	matching record is omitted rather than reported at zero. The bill's `total`
311	is exactly the sum of the subtotals of the listed items. The query is
312	read-only: it writes no usage records, changes no prices or metering
313	conclusions, and never alters already recorded usage — under event replay or
314	recovery the same window and type filter always give the same answer.
315	
316	Both endpoints are tenant-scoped `GET` requests: a missing or empty
317	`X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error` that reveals no usage. Usage and
318	bill data follow the usual tenant isolation, so one tenant can never see
319	another's records under any type filter or window, and another tenant's
320	records never affect this tenant's counts or totals.
321	
322	### Per-record usage history
323	
324	The cumulative usage query reports only per-type totals. A separate endpoint
325	returns the individual usage records themselves, so each billed action can be
326	checked against the moment it occurred:
327	
328	```http
329	GET /usage/records?limit=50
330	X-Tenant-Id: acme
331	```
332	
333	Returns `{"records":[...]}` with the matching records in ascending order of
334	occurrence time; records sharing one instant are ordered by ascending
335	sequence. Each record is:
336	
337	```json
338	{"sequence":7,"type":"execution_started","occurred_at":"2026-09-26T08:30:00.000Z"}
339	```
340	
341	- `sequence` is a stable, strictly increasing positive integer per tenant. It
342	  identifies the record across every query and is never renumbered by a
343	  filter or a page;
344	- `type` is the metered action type;
345	- `occurred_at` is the record's occurrence time as an ISO-8601 UTC string
346	  ending in `Z`.
347	
348	A tenant with no matching records gets the definite empty result
349	`{"records":[]}`, never an error. The response ends with a single newline,
350	like every other JSON endpoint.
351	
352	The endpoint accepts an optional metered-type filter, the same optional
353	closed time window the events and usage queries accept, plus cursor
354	pagination:
355	
356	```http
357	GET /usage/records?type=execution_started,workflow_created&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
358	```
359	
360	- `type` names one metered action type or a comma-separated set of them;
361	  only records whose type is in the set are returned. A single identifier
362	  needs no comma. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown metered
363	  type is a `400 validation_error`; when `type` is absent every type is
364	  returned, exactly as before;
365	- `since` and `until` are ISO-8601 UTC timestamps ending in `Z` and bind a
366	  **closed** interval on each record's occurrence time: a record whose time
367	  equals either boundary is included. When either is absent the corresponding
368	  bound is open; when `since` is later than `until` the window matches
369	  nothing and the definite empty list is returned;
370	- `limit` is **required** and must be a positive integer; a page never
371	  contains more than that many records;
372	- `cursor` is the `sequence` of the previous page's last record; only records
373	  whose `sequence` is strictly greater are returned, so pages neither overlap
374	  nor skip. It is omitted on the first page and must be a positive integer;
375	- the type filter, time window, and pagination apply together as an
376	  intersection, and filtering never changes a record's `sequence`.
377	
378	A malformed timestamp, an unknown, empty, or duplicated `type` entry, a
379	missing or non-positive-integer `limit`, a non-positive-integer `cursor`, a
380	repeated parameter, or any unknown query parameter is a `400
381	validation_error` that writes nothing. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a
382	`400 validation_error` that reveals no records. The query is read-only: it
383	appends no usage records, writes no events, and changes no metering, prices,
384	quotas, or billing conclusions. Records follow the usual tenant isolation, so
385	another tenant's records are never visible under any type filter, window, or
386	page and never affect this tenant's result; replay and recovery leave every
387	recorded sequence, time, and billing conclusion unchanged.
388	
389	### Operational metrics
390	
391	```http
392	GET /metrics
393	X-Tenant-Id: acme
394	```
395	
396	Returns one line of compact JSON summarizing the business facts already
397	recorded for the tenant, ending with the usual single newline. The endpoint
398	is read-only: it appends no events, writes no usage records, and changes no
399	stored data, and it reports only persisted facts — it performs no
400	advancement, approval, recovery, or replay of its own, so those operations
401	never change what a metrics query observes beyond the facts they themselves
402	recorded. A missing or empty `X-Tenant-Id` is a `400 validation_error`, and
403	the metrics follow the usual tenant isolation: another tenant's facts are
404	never visible in any dimension and never affect this tenant's counts. A
405	tenant with no recorded facts at all gets the definite empty result with
406	every dimension at zero — not an error. With no query parameters the answer
407	is every fact recorded for the tenant, byte for byte.
408	
409	The query accepts two optional query parameters, each an ISO-8601 UTC
410	timestamp ending in `Z`:
411	
412	```http
413	GET /metrics?since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z
414	X-Tenant-Id: acme
415	```
416	
417	- `since` and `until` bound a **closed** interval on the facts' occurrence
418	  times: a fact whose time equals `since` or `until` is counted. When either
419	  parameter is absent the corresponding bound is open, so omitting both
420	  counts every recorded fact;
421	- a malformed `since` or `until`, a repeated parameter, or any unknown query
422	  parameter is a `400 validation_error`;
423	- when `since` is later than `until` the request is not an error: the window
424	  simply contains no facts, so every dimension reports its definite zero
425	  result.
426	
427	Each dimension is windowed by the occurrence time of its own fact: node
428	completions, failures, and retry consumption use the time of their recorded
429	node events; delivery outcomes use the delivery record's `occurred_at`
430	(shared by every attempt recorded in it); schedule triggers use the settled
431	period's trigger time; and the status distribution counts an execution at
432	the time it entered its current status — a still-running execution at its
433	start time, and a completed or terminated execution at the time of its
434	completion or termination event.
435	
436	### Export metrics in Prometheus text format
437	
438	```http
439	GET /metrics/export
440	X-Tenant-Id: acme
441	```
442	
443	A read-only tenant-scoped entry point that returns the same counts as the
444	metrics query — including the same optional `since` and `until` filters, the
445	same closed-interval semantics, the same definite zero result for a window
446	with `since` later than `until`, and the same `400 validation_error` for a
447	missing or empty tenant, a malformed timestamp, or an unknown query
448	parameter — rendered in the Prometheus text exposition format
449	(`text/plain; version=0.0.4`). It writes no events and no usage records.
450	
451	Each top-level metrics dimension is one metric family named with the
452	dimension's public key prefixed by `chronicleflow_`. The families appear in
453	the documented top-level key order, and the samples within a family are
454	ordered by ascending label value:
455	
456	- `chronicleflow_status_distribution` — samples carry a `status` label
457	  (`running`, `completed`, `terminated`); only the terminated samples also
458	  carry a `reason` label naming one of the four termination reasons;
459	- `chronicleflow_node_completions`, `chronicleflow_node_failures`, and
460	  `chronicleflow_retry_consumption` — samples carry a `node` label;
461	- `chronicleflow_schedule_triggers` — samples carry a `workflow` label;
462	- `chronicleflow_delivery_succeeded` and `chronicleflow_delivery_failed` —
463	  unlabeled scalar samples.
464	
465	Every value is a decimal integer. A dimension with no facts in the window
466	still exposes a zero-valued sample line (the labeled families expose one
467	unlabeled `0` sample). Every line ends with a newline and the whole document
468	ends with a single newline.
469	
470	The top-level keys appear in this order — status distribution, node
471	completions, node failures, retry consumption, delivery successes, delivery
472	failures, and schedule triggers:
473	
474	```json
475	{"status_distribution":{"running":1,"completed":2,"terminated":{"cancelled":0,"rejected":1,"retries_exhausted":0,"timeout":0}},"node_completions":{"charge":3},"node_failures":{"charge":2},"retry_consumption":{"charge":1},"delivery_succeeded":4,"delivery_failed":1,"schedule_triggers":{"nightly-orders":2}}
476	```
477	
478	- `status_distribution` — the tenant's executions divided into `running`,
479	  `completed`, and `terminated`; `terminated` is further broken down by
480	  termination reason, with every reason (`cancelled`, `rejected`,
481	  `retries_exhausted`, `timeout`) always present, zero when no execution
482	  ended for that reason.
483	- `node_completions` — persisted node completion facts per node identifier.
484	  Condition evaluations and skips are not completions and are never counted;
485	  a loop body node counts once per iteration it completes.
486	- `node_failures` — submitted task failures per node identifier; a loop body
487	  node accumulates each iteration's failures.
488	- `retry_consumption` — the number of times a failed task was re-queued for
489	  another attempt, per node identifier.
490	- `delivery_succeeded` and `delivery_failed` — outbound delivery attempts by
491	  outcome. Every attempt counts exactly once, so a delivery that fails and
492	  then succeeds on a later attempt records one of each.
493	- `schedule_triggers` — schedule periods that created an execution, per
494	  workflow identifier; settling the same period again counts nothing more.
495	
496	All counts are non-negative integers. A dimension with no facts reports zero
497	(or an empty group) rather than being omitted, and the groups within a
498	dimension are ordered by ascending identifier. Migrating an execution to
499	another version does not change attribution: facts recorded before and after
500	the migration accumulate under the same names. The optional `since` and
501	`until` filters and the Prometheus text export are described above.
502	
503	### Health
504	
505	```http
506	GET /health
507	```
508	
509	Returns `{"status":"ok"}`.
510	
511	### Create a workflow
512	
513	```http
514	POST /workflows
515	Idempotency-Key: workflow-request-1
516	
517	{
518	  "id": "order-flow",
519	  "nodes": [
520	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
521	    {"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
522	  ]
523	}
524	```
525	
526	Returns HTTP 201 with the stored workflow. Node identifiers must be unique,
527	dependencies must exist, and cycles are rejected.
528	
529	A workflow definition may carry an optional `version` tag; declaring one
530	enables upgrades and keeps every version. Versioning is described under
531	"Workflow versions" below, and a workflow's stored versions and current
532	version are available through `GET /workflows/{id}`.
533	
534	A workflow may also declare webhook `subscriptions` alongside its nodes:
535	
536	```json
537	{
538	  "id": "order-flow",
539	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
540	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/orders", "events": ["execution_completed"]}]
541	}
542	```
543	
544	See "Webhook notifications" below for the subscription shape and delivery
545	semantics; the subscriptions apply to every execution of the workflow (for a
546	versioned workflow, to executions bound to that version).
547	
548	A workflow may also declare a `schedule` alongside its nodes:
549	
550	```json
551	{
552	  "id": "nightly-orders",
553	  "nodes": [{"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []}],
554	  "schedule": {"interval_seconds": 3600, "input": {"mode": "nightly"}, "missed_policy": "catch_up"}
555	}
556	```
557	
558	See "Schedules" below for the declaration shape and the trigger semantics.
559	
560	Besides `task`, a node may have `kind` set to `condition`:
561	
562	```json
563	{"id": "is_vip", "kind": "condition", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "path": "customer.vip", "equals": true}
564	```
565	
566	`path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into the execution input and `equals`
567	is a JSON scalar (string, number, boolean, or null). A condition is evaluated
568	automatically once its dependencies complete: the input value at `path` is
569	compared with `equals` by JSON type and value, and a missing path evaluates to
570	`false`.
571	
572	A task may carry an optional `run_if` guard:
573	
574	```json
575	{"id": "expedite", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["is_vip"], "run_if": {"condition_id": "is_vip", "expected": true}}
576	```
577	
578	`condition_id` must reference a `condition` node that is also listed in the
579	task's `depends_on`. When the condition's result differs from `expected`, the
580	task is marked as skipped: it receives no output and still satisfies the
581	dependencies of its successors.
582	
583	A task may declare how many times it is retried after a failure:
584	
585	```json
586	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "retries": 3}
587	```
588	
589	`retries` is an integer between 0 and 10 and defaults to 0, meaning the task
590	is attempted only once. Each failure submitted through `advance` consumes one
591	attempt; while retries remain, the task returns to the ready set and is
592	advanced again. When a failure arrives with no retries left, the task is
593	permanently failed and the whole execution terminates with termination reason
594	`retries_exhausted`.
595	
596	A task may instead declare an approval point:
597	
598	```json
599	{"id": "charge", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "approval": {"approvers": ["alice", "bob"]}}
600	```
601	
602	`approval` contains exactly `approvers`, a non-empty array of approver
603	identifier strings without duplicates; an empty list, a duplicate entry, or a
604	non-string entry is a validation error, and only `task` nodes may carry an
605	approval point. When an `advance` reaches a ready task with an approval point,
606	the task does not complete and the submitted output or failure is not
607	consumed: an `approval_requested` event is appended (recording the node, its
608	approvers, and, inside a loop body, the loop id and iteration) and the
609	execution stays `running`, parked in a waiting state returned under
610	`waiting_approval`. Further `advance` calls return the current state without
611	writing output, completing the node, or appending events; only a decision can
612	move the task.
613	
614	### Submit an approval decision
615	
616	```http
617	POST /executions/run-1/decision
618	Idempotency-Key: decision-request-1
619	
620	{"approver":"alice","decision":"approved","output":{"charge_id":"c-3"}}
621	```
622	
623	`decision` is either `approved` or `rejected`. An approved decision carries
624	exactly `approver`, `decision`, and an `output` object; the task completes with
625	that output and its successors become available in the usual way. A rejected
626	decision carries exactly `approver`, `decision`, and a `reason` string; the
627	task is permanently failed (it is listed under `failed_nodes`) and the
628	execution terminates with termination reason `rejected`. Either decision
629	appends an `approval_decided` event with the node, approver, decision, and (on
630	rejection) the reason, and the approval record is kept under `approvals`. A
631	request whose approver is not in the point's approver list is a 409
632	`conflict`, and a malformed body or a decision value other than `approved` or
633	`rejected` is a 400 `validation_error`; neither changes execution state.
634	Repeating the decision that already resolved the most recent approval point —
635	the same approver and decision with the same output or rejection reason —
636	returns the first result and neither advances the node again nor appends
637	another event; any other decision against an execution with no pending
638	approval point is a 409 `conflict`, and deciding a missing execution returns
639	404.
640	
641	While an execution is parked at an approval point it remains `running`, so a
642	cancellation takes effect immediately with the usual `cancelled` termination
643	reason, and a reached timeout terminates it with `timeout`; both dismiss the
644	pending point and the execution then no longer accepts decisions or output.
645	The waiting point, its request and decision events, and the termination
646	reason are rebuilt solely from the event stream on replay, and the parked and
647	decided node boundaries are checkpointed like every other boundary, so
648	waiting points and recorded decisions remain valid after a restart. Approval
649	state is added to an execution only when its workflow declares at least one
650	approval point; workflows without approvals keep exactly the previous state
651	shape and event stream.
652	
653	A node may also have `kind` set to `loop`, describing a bounded repeated
654	segment:
655	
656	```json
657	{"id": "retry", "kind": "loop", "depends_on": ["reserve"], "entry": "attempt", "condition": "keep_trying", "max_iterations": 3}
658	```
659	
660	A loop node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `entry`, `condition`,
661	and `max_iterations`; any other field is rejected as unknown. `entry` names a
662	`task` node, `condition` names a `condition` node, and `max_iterations` is an
663	integer between 1 and 100. The loop body is the repeated segment anchored by
664	the entry task and the condition: it is the entry task, the condition, and
665	every node either anchor reaches through `depends_on`. The two anchors must
666	be connected — the condition gates the entry task (the entry depends on it)
667	or the condition is evaluated after the entry task (it depends on the entry),
668	as in the example above. The body keeps the usual DAG rules and always
669	contains the referenced condition. The loop's own dependencies must be
670	completed or skipped before the first iteration may start, they must not
671	overlap the body, bodies of different loops must not overlap or nest, and
672	nodes outside a body must not depend on nodes inside it (they depend on the
673	loop node instead).
674	
675	When the loop's dependencies are satisfied, the loop evaluates its condition
676	against the execution input (same JSON type and value comparison as condition
677	nodes; a missing path is `false`). If it is `false`, the loop completes with
678	zero iterations and end reason `condition_false`. If it is `true`, the first
679	iteration starts and the body advances one ready task per `advance` call in
680	the usual deterministic order; conditions and `run_if` skips inside the body
681	are re-evaluated every iteration, and task outputs belong only to the current
682	iteration. Once every body node is completed or skipped, the condition is
683	evaluated again: `true` starts the next iteration, `false` ends the loop with
684	`condition_false`, and reaching `max_iterations` ends it with
685	`iteration_limit` after that iteration finishes. Ending the loop completes
686	the loop node and releases the dependencies of its successors. Once the loop
687	has finished, the execution-level `completed_nodes` list also includes every
688	body node that completed in any iteration, each listed only once and in the
689	order of its first completion, followed by the loop node itself; body nodes
690	skipped by a `run_if` guard remain out of the execution-level completed list
691	and are visible only in their iteration record. Body task outputs still
692	belong only to their iterations.
693	
694	Execution state exposes each loop under `loops`: `status`, the
695	`current_iteration`, one entry per iteration with its own `completed_nodes`,
696	`skipped_nodes`, `condition_results`, and `outputs`, and the single
697	`end_reason` (`condition_false` or `iteration_limit`). The event stream
698	records `iteration_started`, `loop_condition_evaluated`, and `loop_completed`
699	events alongside the usual per-node ones, so replay rebuilds loop state
700	exactly.
701	
702	### Dynamic map nodes
703	
704	A `map` node expands at runtime into one task instance per element of a
705	recorded array:
706	
707	```json
708	{"id": "ship", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["collect"],
709	 "source": "collect", "path": "items", "max_instances": 100,
710	 "template": {"id": "ship-item", "retries": 2}}
711	```
712	
713	A map node contains exactly `id`, `kind`, `depends_on`, `source`, `path`,
714	`max_instances`, and `template`; any other field is rejected as unknown.
715	
716	- `source` names a `task` node that is also listed in `depends_on`. Expansion
717	  begins only after every dependency has completed or been skipped; the
718	  element list comes solely from the source task's recorded output.
719	- `path` is a non-empty dot-separated path into that recorded output, using
720	  the same path syntax as a condition.
721	- `max_instances` is a positive integer bounding how many elements may
722	  expand.
723	- `template` describes the single task each instance runs and contains
724	  exactly an `id`, and optionally `retries` (an integer between 0 and 10,
725	  defaulting to 0) and an `approval` point with the same shape a task node
726	  uses. The template id only names the dynamically expanded instances; it
727	  may coincide with a declared node id or with another map's template id.
728	  A map node may also sit inside a loop body, expanding independently in
729	  every iteration (see "Maps inside loop bodies" below).
730	
731	When the dependencies settle, the value at `path` is read once. When it is an
732	array, one instance is created per element; the instances queue in ascending
733	element index order. Each `advance` still settles exactly one ready item, so
734	instances are worked in index order, one per call. An instance is an ordinary
735	task in every other respect: a submitted failure consumes the template's
736	retry bound and re-queues that instance, and a template approval point parks
737	the execution with the instance's `map_id` and `index` recorded, until an
738	approver decides it. Retries and approvals are per instance: results never
739	overwrite another instance.
740	
741	When every instance is completed, the map node completes and its output,
742	recorded both in the node's `outputs` entry and under its `maps` record, is
743	the list of instance outputs in ascending element order; its successors then
744	become available in the usual way.
745	
746	A value that is missing or is not an array expands to zero instances: the map
747	completes with an empty output list and releases its successors immediately.
748	When the array holds more elements than `max_instances`, no instance is
749	created at all: the map node fails permanently, is listed under
750	`failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates with reason `retries_exhausted`
751	under the usual exhaustion semantics.
752	
753	Execution state exposes each map under `maps`: the node's `status`
754	(`pending`, `running`, `completed`, or `failed`), one record per retained
755	instance giving its `index`, `status` (`ready`, `waiting`, `completed`, or
756	`failed`), its `output`, and its `failure_reason` (null except for a
757	permanently failed instance), plus the ordered completed `outputs` list and
758	the node's single `failure_reason`. A `ready` instance that has been
759	rewritten by a successful modify additionally carries that rewritten
760	`input`; every other instance record keeps exactly these fields. The `maps`
761	field is present only when the bound workflow declares a map node outside
762	any loop body; every other execution keeps its previous state shape.
763	
764	The event stream records a `map_expanded` event when expansion happens,
765	carrying the map id and the number of created instances (zero for a missing
766	or non-array value, and zero together with `exceeded` and the observed
767	element count when the bound is exceeded), and a `map_completed` event with
768	the map id and final instance count. Each instance's per-node events —
769	`node_completed`, `node_failed`, and `node_retried`, plus
770	`approval_requested` and `approval_decided` for a template approval point —
771	carry their `map_id` and element `index` alongside the template node id, so
772	replay rebuilds every instance solely from the event stream. Checkpoints are
773	written at instance boundaries, so recovery resumes with the unfinished
774	instances and never repeats an instance output. Per-instance completions and
775	failures count toward the existing node metrics under the template node id,
776	and webhook and queue subscriptions receive instance events exactly like any
777	other node event. Instance deletion and modification add their own
778	`instance_deleted` and `instance_modified` events, and re-expansion adds a
779	`map_reexpanded` event, described under
780	"Delete and modify expanded instances" below.
781	
782	### Maps inside loop bodies
783	
784	A map node may belong to a loop body — it is part of the body exactly when
785	the loop's entry or condition reaches it through `depends_on`, like any
786	other body member:
787	
788	```json
789	{"id": "fanout", "kind": "map", "depends_on": ["attempt"],
790	 "source": "attempt", "path": "items", "max_instances": 10,
791	 "template": {"id": "work", "retries": 1}}
792	```
793	
794	A nested map expands once per iteration, when every dependency of its node
795	is completed or skipped in that iteration, and the element list is read from
796	the source task's output of that same iteration. The expansion rules are the
797	ones of an execution-level map: a missing path or a non-array value expands
798	to zero instances and the map completes for that iteration with an empty
799	output list, so the loop boundary is evaluated as usual; an element count
800	beyond `max_instances` creates no instance at all — the map fails
801	permanently, is listed under `failed_nodes`, and the execution terminates
802	with reason `retries_exhausted` under the usual exhaustion semantics.
803	
804	The expanded instances belong to their iteration only: they queue in
805	ascending element index order and are settled one per `advance`, exactly
806	like execution-level instances, and one iteration's instances never
807	overwrite another iteration's results. An instance is an ordinary task in
808	every other respect — a submitted failure consumes the template's retry
809	bound and re-queues that instance within its iteration, and a template
810	approval point parks the execution until an approver decides it — with no
811	influence from the iteration number.
812	
813	Iteration state exposes each nested map under the iteration record's `maps`
814	field, with the same per-map shape as an execution-level map (`status`, one
815	record per instance, the ordered completed `outputs`, and `failure_reason`);
816	the field is present on every iteration of a loop whose body declares a map
817	node. When a nested map completes, its node enters the iteration's
818	`completed_nodes` and its output list is recorded in the iteration's
819	`outputs`; when the loop finishes, the usual roll-up lists the map node once
820	in the execution-level `completed_nodes`, while its outputs stay with their
821	iterations. An execution-level `maps` field is not created for nested maps.
822	
823	Every event a nested expansion records carries the owning `loop_id` and
824	`iteration` alongside the map id and, for per-instance events, the element
825	`index`: `map_expanded`, `map_completed`, the per-instance `node_completed`,
826	`node_failed`, and `node_retried`, and `approval_requested` and
827	`approval_decided` for a template approval point. The `iteration_started`
828	event of a loop whose body declares map nodes carries the iteration's
829	initial `maps` skeleton, so replay rebuilds every iteration's instance list,
830	status, and ownership solely from the event stream, consistent with the
831	materialized state. Checkpoints are written at each iteration's instance
832	boundaries, so recovery continues the current iteration's unfinished
833	instances and never repeats an instance output. Cancellation, timeouts,
834	leases, retries, and approvals keep their existing semantics, and a nested
835	map never changes an execution's termination reason.
836	
837	Executions whose workflows declare no nested map behave exactly as before:
838	state fields, event contents, and advancement results are unchanged.
839	
840	### Delete and modify expanded instances
841	
842	An expanded dynamic node offers, alongside expansion and per-instance
843	advancement, two instance-level operations and a node-level re-expansion.
844	All three are ordinary idempotent HTTP commands over the same entry points
845	the rest of the service uses; they introduce no second protocol.
846	
847	An instance that has never advanced can be removed, and so can an instance
848	that has permanently failed:
849	
850	```http
851	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/2/delete
852	Idempotency-Key: delete-instance-2
853	
854	{}
855	```
856	
857	The body must be an empty object. Removing an instance drops only that
858	instance's record: every retained instance keeps its element index, its
859	place in the queue, and its advancement order. When the removed instance was
860	the map's last unfinished instance, the node completes under the existing
861	rules with an output list containing only the retained instances' outputs,
862	in ascending element-index order, and its successors unlock as usual. An
863	instance that is waiting on an approval, or has already completed, can never
864	be deleted; attempting it returns `409 conflict` and changes no state. A
865	permanently failed instance is removable after the execution has terminated,
866	but removing it never revives the execution, alters its termination reason,
867	or changes the node's failed conclusion. When every retained instance of a
868	map inside a loop body has ended, the iteration's other nodes advance as
869	usual and the node completes or ends under the existing rules; deleting an
870	instance in one iteration never touches another iteration.
871	
872	An instance that has never advanced can also have its input rewritten
873	before it is worked:
874	
875	```http
876	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/instances/1/modify
877	Idempotency-Key: modify-instance-1
878	
879	{"input":{"address":"742 Evergreen Terrace"}}
880	```
881	
882	The body must contain exactly `input`, an object with the new content; it is
883	validated like every other request body (finite numbers only). The rewrite
884	changes only the parameters used when that one instance is later advanced:
885	it affects no other instance, and the output and history of an instance that
886	has already advanced (waiting, completed, or permanently failed) are
887	immutable — modifying such an instance returns `409 conflict` and changes no
888	state. The rewritten input, including its full float precision and `-0.0`,
889	is stored verbatim.
890	
891	Delete and modify calls on the same instance settle in call order: every
892	call applies to the instance list exactly as the earlier calls left it, and
893	several calls on one instance each take effect independently, one after
894	another. A rewritten instance has still never advanced, so it remains
895	deletable; deleting or modifying an instance an earlier call already
896	removed is a `404 not_found`; and a second rewrite of the same instance
897	records the first rewrite's content as its `before`.
898	
899	Both commands apply to a map nested in a loop body exactly as to an
900	execution-level map: the current running iteration's instances are
901	addressed by the same path, and every event they append carries the owning
902	`loop_id` and `iteration` alongside the map id; an execution-level instance
903	carries no loop context.
904	
905	An out-of-bounds element index, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic
906	`map`, a missing execution, or a cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found`
907	and writes nothing. A missing or mistyped field, a non-object modify
908	`input`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a `400 validation_error`
909	with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a
910	`409 conflict`; repeating the same command with the same key returns the
911	first result and appends no second event.
912	
913	Every successful call appends exactly one event to the execution stream:
914	
915	- an `instance_deleted` event records the action type, the owning dynamic
916	  node under `map_id`, the removed instance's element `index` and `status`
917	  (`ready` or `failed`), and, for a map inside a loop body, the `loop_id`
918	  and `iteration`;
919	- an `instance_modified` event records the action type, the owning
920	  `map_id`, the instance `index`, the content `before` the rewrite (`null`
921	  for an instance that had never been rewritten) and `after` it, and the
922	  same loop context when the instance belongs to an iteration.
923	
924	Replay rebuilds the instance list, every instance's status and ownership,
925	and each rewrite solely from the event stream: a delete drops the recorded
926	instance (and the subsequent `map_completed`, when the deletion finished the
927	node, completes it with the retained outputs), and a modify applies the
928	rewritten input to that one instance, so the rebuilt state is exactly the
929	materialized state. A checkpoint is written at the instance boundary of
930	every successful delete or modify; after a restart recovery continues the
931	unfinished instances, repeats no instance output, and never resurrects a
932	deleted instance. The operations change no advancement conclusion or
933	termination semantics: cancellation, timeouts, approvals, leases, retries,
934	and retry exhaustion keep their existing behavior. Executions that never
935	use deletion, modification, or re-expansion keep exactly their current
936	state fields, event contents, and advancement results.
937	
938	### Re-expand a dynamic node
939	
940	A dynamic node that has already expanded can be expanded again on demand —
941	above all to regenerate its instance list after deletions:
942	
943	```http
944	POST /executions/run-1/maps/ship/reexpand
945	Idempotency-Key: reexpand-1
946	
947	{}
948	```
949	
950	(The same operation is also accepted at `.../maps/ship/expand`.) The body
951	must be an empty object. Re-expansion reads the element list again from the
952	source task's recorded output — the same recorded output the first
953	expansion read, which never changes once recorded — and regenerates the
954	instance list from it: every previous instance record is replaced, and the
955	fresh instances queue from element index zero in ascending order. The
956	regenerated instances are ordinary instances in every respect: they are
957	deleted, modified, advanced, retried, and approved through the same entries
958	and with exactly the same behavior as a first expansion, and their retry
959	bounds start from zero.
960	
961	Every successful call appends exactly one `map_reexpanded` event, recording
962	the action type, the owning dynamic node under `map_id`, and the number of
963	generated instances under `instance_count`; for a map inside a loop body
964	the event also carries the owning `loop_id` and `iteration`, and only the
965	current running iteration's expansion is replaced. A node that had
966	completed returns to `running`: it leaves `completed_nodes`, its recorded
967	output entry is discarded, and when the regenerated instances have all
968	completed the node completes again under the existing rules, its result
969	list holding only the finally retained instances' outputs in ascending
970	element-index order. An empty element list completes the node again at
971	once with an empty output list, exactly like a zero-element first
972	expansion.
973	
974	Re-expansion is rejected with `409 conflict` and writes nothing when the
975	node has not expanded yet, when it has permanently failed, when one of its
976	instances is waiting on an approval decision, when the execution has
977	already completed, or when a nested map's loop is not currently running.
978	A terminated execution's unfinished node may still be re-expanded; doing so
979	never revives the execution or alters its termination reason. A missing
980	execution, a reference to a node that is not a dynamic `map`, or a
981	cross-tenant reference is a `404 not_found` and writes nothing. A
982	non-empty or non-object body, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
983	`400 validation_error` with no partial write. Reusing an idempotency key
984	from another operation is a `409 conflict`; repeating the same call with
985	the same key returns the first result and appends no second event. Replay
986	rebuilds the regenerated instance list, statuses, and ownership solely
987	from the event stream, a checkpoint is written at the re-expansion
988	boundary, and recovery after a restart continues the unfinished
989	regenerated instances — repeating no instance output and never resurrecting
990	an instance that stayed deleted.
991	
992	### Workflow versions
993	
994	A workflow can declare a version tag alongside its nodes:
995	
996	```json
997	{
998	  "id": "order-flow",
999	  "version": "2026-09-25",
1000	  "nodes": [
1001	    {"id": "reserve", "kind": "task", "depends_on": []},
1002	    {"id": "ship", "kind": "task", "depends_on": ["reserve"]}
1003	  ]
1004	}
1005	```
1006	
1007	`version` is an optional non-empty string of at most 100 characters, validated
1008	like every other identifier. Posting it when the workflow does not yet exist
1009	creates the workflow with that version; posting another definition with a new
1010	`version` to the same `id` adds a new version without touching the previous
1011	ones — the workflow keeps its entire history, and every stored version remains
1012	usable. The most recently added version becomes the workflow's current
1013	version. Posting a definition without a `version` to an existing workflow
1014	still conflicts, and reusing a version tag already stored for the same
1015	workflow is a `409 conflict`; either rejection writes nothing.
1016	
1017	A version declaration may also carry `subscriptions` and a `schedule`,
1018	validated exactly like at creation. Subscriptions are attached to the
1019	declared version and apply only to executions bound to it; a version without
1020	subscriptions replaces none, and other versions' subscriptions stay intact.
1021	Declaring a `schedule` on an added version replaces the workflow's single
1022	schedule plan in the usual way (re-anchored, pause flag kept).
1023	
1024	An execution created without an explicit `version` binds to the workflow's
1025	current version at the moment it starts:
1026	
1027	```http
1028	POST /executions
1029	Idempotency-Key: execution-versioned
1030	
1031	{"id":"run-v2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{}}
1032	```
1033	
1034	An execution may instead name the version it wants:
1035	
1036	```json
1037	{"id":"run-v1","workflow_id":"order-flow","version":"2026-08-01","input":{}}
1038	```
1039	
1040	Naming a version that does not exist for the workflow is a missing-resource
1041	`404 not_found`, exactly like naming a workflow that does not exist; the
1042	execution is not created. Everything about an execution follows its bound
1043	version: ready-node selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval
1044	points, retry counts, leases, and the subscriptions that fire for its events.
1045	Adding a new version never interrupts an execution already running: an
1046	execution started before the upgrade keeps advancing on its old version to
1047	completion or termination. Its checkpoints are snapshots of the same state,
1048	recovery rebuilds from the bound version, and replay rebuilds state and the
1049	version binding solely from its event stream; recorded events and historical
1050	conclusions never change.
1051	
1052	A versioned execution's state carries its `version` tag, and its
1053	`execution_started` event records the same tag; querying it therefore shows
1054	which version it is bound to. A workflow that never declares a version, and an
1055	execution of one, keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
1056	stream with no added field.
1057	
1058	The definition query lists every version and the current one:
1059	
1060	```http
1061	GET /workflows/order-flow
1062	```
1063	
1064	```json
1065	{"current_version":"2026-09-25","id":"order-flow","versions":[
1066	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-08-01"},
1067	  {"id":"order-flow","nodes":[...],"version":"2026-09-25"}
1068	]}
1069	```
1070	
1071	Versions are returned in declaration order; each entry is the stored
1072	definition with its `version` tag. A workflow that never declared a version
1073	returns a single untagged entry and `current_version: null`. A missing
1074	workflow returns 404 `not_found`. Cross-tenant references are missing
1075	resources as usual.
1076	
1077	### Migrate a running execution to another version
1078	
1079	```http
1080	POST /executions/run-v1/migrate
1081	Idempotency-Key: migrate-request-1
1082	
1083	{"version":"2026-09-25"}
1084	```
1085	
1086	A running execution can be explicitly moved to another declared version of
1087	the same workflow; after the call it keeps advancing under the new version.
1088	The body must contain exactly `version`, a non-empty version identifier that
1089	names a stored version of the execution's workflow. On success a
1090	`version_migrated` event is appended to the event stream — it records the
1091	`from_version`, the `to_version`, and the structural skeleton of the target
1092	revision (its `loops`, and, when it declares approval points, its
1093	`waiting_approval` and `approvals` fields) — and a checkpoint of the rebound
1094	state is written at that same node boundary. The execution's state then
1095	carries the target version.
1096	
1097	Everything that follows uses the target version's definition: ready-node
1098	selection, condition evaluation, loop rounds, approval points, retries, and
1099	the workflow subscriptions that fire for later events. Everything recorded
1100	before the migration is kept exactly as-is: prior events, node outputs,
1101	condition conclusions, and per-iteration history are never rewritten. Loops
1102	introduced by the target definition begin in their initial pending state; a
1103	loop the old definition knew keeps its recorded iterations and conclusion.
1104	Replay rebuilds the migration point and version binding solely from the
1105	event stream, and after a restart recovery continues on the migrated version
1106	from the migration checkpoint, so checkpoints and materialized state agree.
1107	
1108	An execution parked at an approval point may also be migrated: the waiting
1109	point keeps its recorded node and approver list unchanged (only a recorded
1110	approver may still decide it), and once the decision lands the subsequent
1111	advancement follows the target version. Executions that are never migrated
1112	keep advancing on the version they started with to completion or
1113	termination; adding versions never moves them. An execution of a workflow
1114	that never declared a version cannot name a target, and such workflows and
1115	their executions keep exactly the previous behavior, state shape, and event
1116	content.
1117	
1118	The response is the updated execution state. Migrating a `completed` or
1119	`terminated` execution returns `409 conflict` and changes nothing. A missing
1120	execution or a target version that does not exist for the workflow returns
1121	`404 not_found`; a cross-tenant reference is the same missing resource. A
1122	missing or mistyped `version`, an unknown field, or a non-finite number is a
1123	`400 validation_error`. Migrating a running execution to the version it is
1124	already bound to returns the current state as-is, appending no event and
1125	writing no checkpoint; a `completed` or `terminated` execution instead
1126	returns `409 conflict` even when the target version is exactly the one it is
1127	bound to. Reusing an idempotency key for another operation is a `409
1128	conflict`. The migration event is listed directly by the per-execution
1129	events query, and node outputs produced after the migration belong to the
1130	target version's definition. Approver-list validation, lease renewal, and
1131	delivery history keep their existing semantics before and after a migration.
1132	
1133	### Start an execution
1134	
1135	```http
1136	POST /executions
1137	Idempotency-Key: execution-request-1
1138	
1139	{"id":"run-1","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{"order_id":"o-7"}}
1140	```
1141	
1142	Returns HTTP 201. The execution starts in `running` state. Without an
1143	explicit `version`, it binds to the workflow's current version at start time;
1144	naming a `version` binds to that one instead (and a missing version is a
1145	`404 not_found`). See "Workflow versions" for the binding and upgrade rules.
1146	
1147	An execution may declare a timeout:
1148	
1149	```json
1150	{"id":"run-2","workflow_id":"order-flow","input":{},"timeout_seconds":30}
1151	```
1152	
1153	`timeout_seconds` is a positive number of seconds counted from the moment the
1154	execution starts. Once the deadline passes, the execution terminates with
1155	termination reason `timeout` and no longer accepts output. Executions without
1156	a timeout never expire.
1157	
1158	An execution may also declare its own webhook `subscriptions`, which apply in
1159	addition to the ones its workflow declares:
1160	
1161	```json
1162	{
1163	  "id": "run-3",
1164	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
1165	  "input": {},
1166	  "subscriptions": [{"url": "https://hooks.example.com/ops", "events": ["node_completed"], "max_attempts": 3}]
1167	}
1168	```
1169	
1170	### List workflows
1171	
1172	```http
1173	GET /workflows?limit=50
1174	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1175	```
1176	
1177	Enumerates the workflows declared in the request's namespace. The response
1178	is `{"workflows":[{"id":"order-flow"}, ...]}`: one entry per workflow, each
1179	carrying its identifier, in ascending identifier order. A namespace with no
1180	workflows gets the definite empty result `{"workflows":[]}`, not an error.
1181	The query is read-only: it creates nothing, appends no events, and records
1182	no usage, so repeating it returns the same answer and changes no stored
1183	state.
1184	
1185	The list is paged with a keyset cursor:
1186	
1187	- `limit` — required; the maximum number of entries in the page, a positive
1188	  integer. The page never holds more entries than the limit;
1189	- `cursor` — optional; the identifier of the previous page's last entry.
1190	  Only entries whose identifier sorts strictly after the cursor are
1191	  returned, so paging with the previous page's last identifier yields
1192	  consecutive pages that neither overlap nor skip. A cursor past the end
1193	  returns the definite empty list.
1194	
1195	### List executions
1196	
1197	```http
1198	GET /executions?workflow_id=order-flow&status=terminated&termination_reason=timeout&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=run-41&limit=50
1199	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1200	```
1201	
1202	Enumerates the executions in the request's namespace in ascending execution
1203	identifier order. The response is `{"executions":[...]}`; each entry carries
1204	the execution `id`, its `workflow_id`, its `status` (`running`, `completed`,
1205	or `terminated`, always a string), its `termination_reason` (one of the
1206	four termination reasons for a terminated execution, otherwise `null`), and
1207	its `created_at` (the ISO-8601 UTC creation timestamp ending in `Z`), in
1208	that stable key order. A namespace with no executions gets the definite
1209	empty result `{"executions":[]}`. Like the workflows list this query is
1210	read-only and never settles a due timeout, appends an event, writes a
1211	checkpoint, or records usage, so repeated calls return the same answer and
1212	change no state or metering conclusion.
1213	
1214	The same `limit` and `cursor` pagination applies, with the cursor taken
1215	from the previous page's last execution identifier. In addition, five
1216	filters may be combined, and every given filter must match:
1217	
1218	- `workflow_id` — only executions of that workflow. Referencing a workflow
1219	  the namespace does not contain, including one owned by another tenant, is
1220	  the usual `404 not_found` and reveals nothing about its existence;
1221	- `status` — only executions in that lifecycle status. A value other than
1222	  `running`, `completed`, or `terminated` is a `400 validation_error`;
1223	- `termination_reason` — only executions that terminated for exactly that
1224	  reason. The filter is meaningful solely for terminated executions:
1225	  running and completed executions never appear under it, even when other
1226	  filters are given alongside it. An unknown reason is a
1227	  `400 validation_error`;
1228	- `since` and `until` — the same closed creation-time bounds the events and
1229	  metrics queries accept: each is an ISO-8601 UTC timestamp ending in `Z`,
1230	  and an execution whose `created_at` equals `since` or `until` is
1231	  returned. When either parameter is absent the corresponding bound is
1232	  open, so omitting both returns exactly the unfiltered list; a malformed
1233	  timestamp is a `400 validation_error`. When `since` is later than
1234	  `until` the window matches nothing and the result is the definite empty
1235	  list, not an error.
1236	
1237	Both list endpoints follow the usual tenant scope: omitting
1238	`X-Tenant-Id` keeps the single legacy namespace, and a tenant sees only its
1239	own workflows and executions under every combination of filters. Every
1240	parameter may appear at most once; a repeated parameter, an unknown
1241	parameter, a missing `limit`, or a `limit` that is not a positive integer is
1242	a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing.
1243	
1244	### Inspect an execution
1245	
1246	```http
1247	GET /executions/run-1
1248	GET /executions/run-1/events
1249	GET /executions/run-1/checkpoints
1250	```
1251	
1252	The first endpoint returns the materialized state. The second returns the
1253	ordered event stream. The third returns the ordered checkpoints; each entry
1254	gives its `sequence`, the `event_sequence` position it was taken at, the full
1255	`state` summary, and `created_at`.
1256	
1257	The events query is read-only: it appends no events, records no usage, and
1258	changes no state, so advancement, approvals, recovery, and replay never alter
1259	what it observes. With no query parameters it returns the complete ordered
1260	event list exactly as before. It also accepts optional filter and pagination
1261	parameters, which combine as an intersection:
1262	
1263	```http
1264	GET /executions/run-1/events?types=node_completed,node_failed&since=2026-09-26T08:00:00.000Z&until=2026-09-26T09:00:00.000Z&cursor=12&limit=50
1265	```
1266	
1267	- `types` — a comma-separated set of event types; only events whose type is
1268	  in the set are returned. An empty entry, a duplicate entry, or an unknown
1269	  event type is a `400 validation_error`;
1270	- `since` and `until` — the same closed-interval occurrence-time bounds the
1271	  metrics query accepts: an event whose time equals either boundary is
1272	  returned. When `since` is later than `until` the window matches nothing and
1273	  the result is an empty list, not an error;
1274	- `cursor` — the sequence of the last event of the previous page; only events
1275	  with a strictly greater sequence are returned;
1276	- `limit` — the maximum number of events in the page, in ascending sequence
1277	  order.
1278	
1279	Every parameter may appear at most once; a repeated parameter, an unknown
1280	parameter, a malformed timestamp, or a cursor or limit that is not a positive
1281	integer is a `400 validation_error` that writes nothing. Filtering never
1282	renumbers events, so paging with `cursor` set to the previous page's last
1283	sequence yields consecutive pages that neither overlap nor skip. A filter
1284	that matches nothing returns the definite empty result `{"events":[]}`, and
1285	querying a missing or another tenant's execution is the usual
1286	`404 not_found`.
1287	
1288	### Webhook notifications
1289	
1290	Subscriptions declared on a workflow or an execution deliver outbound webhook
1291	messages when business events occur. Each webhook subscription contains exactly:
1292	
1293	- `url`: a non-empty `http` or `https` address to POST to;
1294	- `events`: a non-empty array of event types without duplicates, drawn from
1295	  `node_completed`, `execution_completed`, `execution_terminated`, and
1296	  `approval_decided` (a termination is the same event type whatever its
1297	  reason);
1298	- `timeout_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds to wait for each
1299	  delivery attempt, defaulting to 5;
1300	- `max_attempts` (optional): an integer between 1 and 10, defaulting to 1.
1301	
1302	Any other field, a missing `url` or `events`, a mistyped value, an empty or
1303	duplicated event list, an unknown event type, an empty or non-http(s) `url`,
1304	a non-finite number, a non-positive timeout or attempt count, or more than
1305	ten attempts is a 400 `validation_error` and rejects the whole request — no
1306	workflow, execution, or subscription is partially written. A subscription
1307	may instead declare a queue target (`queue` instead of `url`); see "Queue
1308	subscriptions" below.
1309	
1310	When a subscribed event occurs, a JSON message is POSTed to each matching
1311	target immediately: the body carries `event_type`, `execution_id`, and the
1312	event's details (such as `node_id` for a completed node or `approver` for an
1313	approval decision). Each delivery request carries an `Idempotency-Key`
1314	header; retries of the same event reuse the same key, and different events
1315	never share a key. A delivery is attempted at most the subscription's
1316	`max_attempts` times, with an increasing backoff between attempts. An
1317	unreachable target, a timeout, or a non-2xx response marks the attempt as
1318	failed, but a failed delivery never changes the outcome of the call that
1319	triggered it.
1320	
1321	Deliveries do not append execution events, do not add fields to the execution
1322	state, and are never triggered by replay, recovery, or queries, so
1323	checkpoints and replay conclusions are unaffected. An execution that declares
1324	no subscriptions keeps exactly the same state, event stream, and advancement
1325	results as before.
1326	
1327	### Inspect the delivery history
1328	
1329	```http
1330	GET /executions/run-1/deliveries
1331	```
1332	
1333	Returns `{"deliveries": [...]}` in the order the events occurred. Each record
1334	gives its `sequence`, the subscription `url`, the `event_type`, the
1335	`event_sequence` that triggered it, the delivery `idempotency_key`, the final
1336	`status` (`delivered` or `failed`), the `attempt_count`, an `attempts` list
1337	recording each try's `status_code` or `error` (so a retry that eventually
1338	succeeds is visible attempt by attempt), and `occurred_at`. Querying the
1339	history of a missing execution returns 404 `not_found` and records nothing.
1340	Every delivery attempt is recorded, including one whose history record itself
1341	could not be written: such a failure is not swallowed — it is retried once in
1342	a fresh write carrying `status` `failed` and a `persistence_error` describing
1343	the write failure, so the attempt remains visible whenever the database can
1344	accept it (and is logged rather than silently dropped if it cannot).
1345	
1346	### Queue subscriptions
1347	
1348	A subscription may declare a queue target instead of a webhook `url`:
1349	
1350	```json
1351	{
1352	  "id": "run-4",
1353	  "workflow_id": "order-flow",
1354	  "input": {},
1355	  "subscriptions": [{"queue": "order-events", "events": ["node_completed"], "visibility_seconds": 60}]
1356	}
1357	```
1358	
1359	A queue subscription contains exactly:
1360	
1361	- `queue`: a non-empty queue name of any length;
1362	- `events`: the same non-empty event-type list a webhook subscription takes;
1363	- `visibility_seconds` (optional): a positive number of seconds a pulled
1364	  message stays invisible while awaiting acknowledgement, defaulting to 30.
1365	
1366	Exactly one of `url` and `queue` must be present in a subscription. Any
1367	other field, a missing or invalid `events` list, an empty queue name, or a
1368	non-positive or non-finite visibility timeout is a 400 `validation_error`
1369	that rejects the whole request without partial writes. Queue names are
1370	unique per tenant across declarations: declaring a name that another
1371	workflow or execution of the same tenant already declared is a 409
1372	`conflict`, while different tenants may reuse the same names freely.
1373	
1374	A workflow or an execution may declare several queue targets. Every
1375	execution gets its own queues — those declared on the workflow revision it
1376	is bound to, plus those it declares itself — and when a subscribed event
1377	occurs, a message carrying the event type and its details is appended to
1378	each matching queue of that execution, in occurrence order. The append is
1379	atomic with the event itself: a rejected operation leaves no queued message
1380	behind. Each message carries an idempotency key that is deterministic per
1381	event and queue: every delivery of the same message reuses the same key,
1382	and different events never share a key. Queues add no fields to the
1383	execution state and append no events, and replay, recovery, and queries
1384	never enqueue. Executions that declare no queue targets behave exactly as
1385	before.
1386	
1387	### Inspect the queue state
1388	
1389	```http
1390	GET /executions/run-4/queues
1391	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1392	```
1393	
1394	Returns `{"queues": [...]}` with one entry per queue of the execution, in
1395	declaration order; an execution with no queue targets gets the definite
1396	empty result `{"queues": []}`. Each entry gives its `queue` name, the
1397	`visibility_seconds` in effect, and the queue's `messages` in entry order —
1398	an empty list for a queue that never received a message. Each message record
1399	gives its `sequence` (the entry order), the `event_type` and
1400	`event_sequence` that produced it, the event `payload`, the message
1401	`idempotency_key`, the `delivery_count`, a `deliveries` list recording every
1402	delivery with its `delivery` number and `delivered_at` time, the
1403	`enqueued_at` time, and the current `status` (`pending`, `delivered`, or
1404	`acknowledged`). Querying the queues of a missing execution — including one
1405	owned by another tenant — is the usual 404 `not_found`.
1406	
1407	### Pull messages from a queue
1408	
1409	```http
1410	POST /executions/run-4/queues/order-events/pull
1411	Idempotency-Key: pull-request-1
1412	X-Tenant-Id: acme
1413	
1414	{}
1415	```
1416	
1417	The body must be an empty object. The response is `{"messages": [...]}`: the
1418	currently pending messages in entry order, each rendered like the message
1419	records of the queue state query. A pulled message becomes invisible for the
1420	queue's visibility timeout; if it is not acknowledged by then, it returns to
1421	the pending set and is delivered again — the queue semantics are at least
1422	once, and every delivery is recorded in the message's delivery history.
1423	Pulling an empty queue, or one whose messages are all invisible, is a
1424	definite empty result `{"messages": []}`, not an error. Every delivery to
1425	the caller is metered as one `delivery_attempted` usage record, exactly like
1426	an outbound webhook attempt, and counts toward the tenant's bill.
1427	
1428	### Acknowledge a message
